abstract: In small-scale longline fishing, a small crew must simultaneously and cooperatively perform vessel maneuvering, fish school detection, and depth adjustment of the fishing gear. This study presents the conceptual design and simulation-based evaluation of “Mamball” a pneumatically driven underwater device designed to adjust the depth of longline fishing gear. Compressed air supplied from the vessel expels seawater from an internal tank, thereby altering the effective buoyancy. A feedback loop is established using a depth sensor, and a ring-shaped wing is proposed as an auxiliary lift actuator. A lumped-parameter model was developed to relate the supply pressure, internal water level displacement, volume of water expelled, and vertical motion. We compared conventional Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) control with Integral-Proportional-Derivative (I-PD) control using representative step response simulations from an initial depth of 2 m to a target depth of 5 m. When no delay was set, the PID response approached the target value in approximately 10 s but exhibited overshoot. When a 0.5-second delay was applied, the PID response took approximately 50 seconds to settle near the target value, whereas the I-PD response approached the target value in about 20 seconds without significant overshoot. Under the single condition reported in this study, the characteristic response time was reduced by approximately 60%. While these results support further research and development of this concept, they do not constitute experimental validation. Future work will require parameter identification of the pneumatic and hydrodynamic systems, reproducible controller tuning, and controlled tank and sea trials.

sections.content:
While small-scale fisheries support food supply and coastal communities, many tasks must be carried out with limited personnel and equipment. Therefore, smart fishing technologies are being researched as a means to integrate sensing, decision support, positioning, and automation into fishing activities [1]. For small-scale fishermen in particular, low-cost tracking and sensing systems are crucial, and the initial cost of equipment, maintainability, and ease of repair can be just as important as the device’s nominal performance [2].

 In longline fishing, a main line equipped with numerous branch lines and hooks is used. The depth of the fishing gear is influenced by vessel motion, ocean currents, the shape of the main line, sinkers, floats, and the method of deploying the gear. Field observations and dynamic analyses have shown that the actual depth reached by floating longline gear can differ significantly from simple static estimates [3,4]. Therefore, in order to position the hooks near detected fish schools, an experienced operator must appropriately adjust the vessel’s speed and gear manipulation.

 Figure 1 illustrates the operational configuration assumed in this study. A main line equipped with multiple branch lines is deployed from the vessel, and the target fish school is located at a certain depth below it. The automation addressed in this study is not limited to mere vessel navigation. The objective is to actively adjust the depth of the fishing gear itself when ocean currents, vessel speed, or loads acting on the longline change.

 Fig. 1. Conceptual arrangement of the vessel, main line, branch lines, hooks, and fish school in longline fishing. The device proposed in this study is not intended to replace the entire fishing system but rather to adjust the vertical position of the fishing gear.

 Underwater gliders are a representative technology that enables efficient vertical movement through variable buoyancy [5–8]. Their depth and pitch movements are modeled and controlled using feedback control that takes into account changes in buoyancy, hydrodynamic forces, and vehicle attitude [9,10].However, conventional autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and underwater gliders may be too costly or have overly complex mechanical structures to be used as devices deployed in large numbers on longlines. Research on small variable-buoyancy systems and depth-control platforms has demonstrated that compact buoyancy control mechanisms are feasible [11–13]. On the other hand, the mechanisms and mission requirements of these systems differ from those of moored fishing devices.

sections.content:
In this study, we examine a device that receives pneumatic pressure from a vessel as a cost-effective alternative. The device consists of a simple underwater tank, a depth sensor, and the proposed annular wing. Due to its nearly spherical shape, this device has been named “Mamball” after the Japanese word for “ocean sunfish” (manbou). In the future, it is envisioned that multiple Mamballs will be distributed along a longline and controlled to maintain different target depths.

sections.title: 1.2 Research Issues and Objectives
1. Proposal of a system architecture that adjusts the depth of longline fishing gear using air pressure supplied from a vessel.
2. Development of a lumped-parameter model correlating supply pressure, internal water level displacement, buoyancy, and vertical motion.
3. Comparison of PID and I-PD control structures under illustrative conditions with a 0.5-second actuation delay.

blocks.html: In the proposed system, one or more Mamball devices are deployed along the longline fishing gear. Each device is designed to maintain multiple hooks near a specified depth by varying the local vertical forces acting on the longline. Figure 2 illustrates the concept using multiple devices. If each device can be controlled independently, it should be possible to vary the depth distribution of the longline to track fish schools or to avoid contact with the seafloor. However, to realize such operation, it is necessary to examine the interactions between adjacent devices, the main line tension, and the routing of the pneumatic tubes.

blocks.html: Compressed air is supplied from a compressor mounted on the vessel via a proportional valve and air tubing. When the supply pressure exceeds the opposing hydrostatic pressure and fluid losses, the compressed air acts on the internal water surface, expelling seawater through the lower outlet. As a result, the internal air volume increases.In the conceptual model, it is assumed that the net upward force increases due to the volume change caused by the discharge and the reduction in the mass of seawater retained inside. Conversely, lowering the tank pressure causes seawater to flow back in, reducing the net buoyancy.

 The motion of the internal water is given by

\(m\ddot{x}+{c}_{x}\dot{x}={F}_{1}-{F}_{2}.\)(3)

 In Equation (3), m represents the inertia due to the concentrated mass of water retained in the tank, and \({c}_{x}\dot{x}\) represents the combined resistance due to the motion of the port, fittings, and interfaces. Let \(r\left(t\right)\) denote target depth, \(y\left(t\right)\) measured depth, and \(e\left(t\right)=r\left(t\right)-y\left(t\right)\) tracking error. In a conventional PID structure, all three actions operate on the error:

\({u}_{PID}\left(t\right)={K}_{p}e\left(t\right)+{K}_{i}\int_{0}^{t} e\left(\tau \right)\,d\tau +{K}_{d}\frac{de\left(t\right)}{dt}.\)(11)

 The proportional term responds to the current error, the integral term removes accumulated steady-state deviations, and the derivative term responds to the rate of change of the error. If the target value changes in a step, that change is directly transmitted to the proportional and derivative paths, which may result in strong transient control commands.

 In the I-PD structure, the integral action acts on the tracking error, while the proportional and derivative actions act on the measured output.

\({u}_{IPD}\left(t\right)={K}_{i}\int_{0}^{t} e\left(\tau \right)\,d\tau -{K}_{p}y\left(t\right)-{K}_{d}\frac{dy\left(t\right)}{dt}.\)(12)

 In the structure shown in Equation (12), direct excitation of the proportional and derivative paths caused by a setpoint step is reduced. I-PD is a variant of the more general two-degree-of-freedom PID structure [14,15]. Whether I-PD is effective for a specific system depends on the controlled system, gain tuning, constraints, disturbance suppression objectives, and measurement noise, among other factors.

 Figure 7 compares the two control structures. In the PID block diagram, the error is fed into the entire controller. In contrast, in the I-PD block diagram, only the integral branch is driven by the error, while the proportional and derivative feedback are derived from the measurement depth. To conduct a quantitative comparison in an academic paper, it is necessary to explicitly specify the gains, filters, saturation limits, and tuning criteria for both structures.

 Fig. 7. Block diagrams of (a) conventional PID control and (b) I-PD control. In the I-PD structure, the proportional and derivative actions are excluded from the setpoint path.

blocks.html: Representative simulations demonstrate that, when delays exist in pneumatic actuation, the structure of the setpoint path can influence the control response. In conventional PID control, a setpoint step immediately contributes to the proportional action and, in the absence of filters or similar elements, also contributes to a derivative kick.In contrast, in I-PD control, since the proportional and derivative actions depend on the measurement depth, it is possible to mitigate the control commands generated when the setpoint changes. sections.title: 4.5 Model Limitations and Verification Roadmap
1. Pneumatic bench tests: Measure valve commands, inlet pressure, air flow rate, water level displacement, air leakage, and time delays for the assumed pressure range and tube length.
2. Static buoyancy test: Measure the force in response to internal water level displacement and verify the relationship assumed in Equation (6).
3. Single-unit tank test: Identify vertical drag, added mass, tank recovery behavior, and depth sensor noise, and compare model predictions with measured transient responses.
4. Controller Comparison Test: Using the specified tuning procedure and common constraints, compare PID and I-PD control under multiple test conditions and various disturbance conditions.
5. Towing and longline coupling tests: Measure annular lift, longline tension, tube torsion, and interactions with actual fishing gear.

sections.content:
This study presents a conceptual design and control evaluation based on simulations of the Mamball, a pneumatically driven device designed to adjust the depth of longline fishing gear. In the proposed mechanism, compressed air supplied from the vessel is used to vary the volume of seawater in an internal tank, forming a feedback loop using a depth sensor. In addition, to accommodate attitude, tube torsion, and auxiliary vertical actuation, we proposed a passively stabilized tank, a rotatable tube joint, and annular wings.

 A lumped-parameter model was used to relate the supply pressure, internal water level displacement, residual water mass, discharged water volume, buoyancy, and device depth. In the representative response data available, PID control without a delay approached the target depth of 5 m from an initial depth of 2 m in approximately 10 s but exhibited overshoot. When a 0.5-second delay was included, it took approximately 50 seconds for the PID response to settle near the target value, whereas the I-PD response approached the target value in about 20 seconds without significant overshoot. The reduction in the characteristic time calculated for this single condition was approximately 60%.

While these findings demonstrate the value of further investigating this system, they do not prove its experimental performance or general robustness. To submit this as a reproducible technical study, it is necessary to explicitly specify the numerical model, controller gains, simulation conditions, and performance evaluation criteria. Subsequently, buoyancy generation, aerodynamics, hydrodynamics, controller performance, reliability, and safety must be verified through bench tests, tank tests, towing tests, and limited sea trials.
